question: What are the main HTTP methods and what is each used for?
title: HTTP Methods Overview
direct_answer: The main HTTP methods are GET (read), POST (create), PUT (full update), PATCH (partial update), and DELETE (remove). Each maps to a CRUD operation and has specific safety and idempotency characteristics.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic REST knowledge and ability to map HTTP methods to operations
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying POST is for all writes or confusing PUT vs PATCH
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain idempotency for each method and the safe vs unsafe distinction

sections.title: HTTP Method Semantics
sections.content: HTTP methods define the intended operation on a resource. REST uses these standardized verbs so that API consumers know what to expect. The method choice affects caching, idempotency, and how intermediaries (proxies, browsers) handle requests.

sections.title: Methods and Their Uses
content: GET: Read resource — safe and idempotent, can be cached
POST: Create resource — not idempotent (calling twice creates two records)
PUT: Full update — idempotent (calling multiple times has same effect)
PATCH: Partial update — idempotent in practice, updates only specified fields
DELETE: Remove resource — idempotent (deleting twice returns 404, same end state)
HEAD: Like GET but returns only headers — used to check resource existence
OPTIONS: Returns allowed methods — used in CORS preflight

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: The five main HTTP methods map to CRUD operations. GET reads data and is safe — no side effects. POST creates resources and isn't idempotent, so calling it twice creates two records. PUT does a full replacement — if you PUT with only some fields, the missing ones get nulled. PATCH is for partial updates, sending only the changed fields. DELETE removes the resource. A key distinction: GET and HEAD are safe methods because they don't modify state. GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent — calling them multiple times produces the same result.

followup_questions: What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?
What does idempotent mean and which methods are idempotent?
When would you use POST vs PUT to create a resource?

seo.metaTitle: HTTP Methods GET POST PUT PATCH DELETE | Java Backend Interview
seo.metaDescription: Learn HTTP methods, their uses, and idempotency for REST API interviews. Java backend fresher prep.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API for a todo app with GET, POST, PUT, DELETE endpoints
speakable_v2.hook: HTTP methods are the verbs of REST — know what each one promises and you'll never misuse them.

beats.text: HTTP methods define the intended operation on a resource. REST uses these standardized verbs so that API consumers know what to expect. The method choice also tells browsers, proxies, and clients whether a request is safe to cache or retry.

Without agreed method semantics, every API would invent its own verbs in URIs. HTTP methods give a universal vocabulary — GET always reads, DELETE always removes — so any client can reason about any REST API.

items: GET: reads a resource — safe (no side effects) and idempotent; responses can be cached
POST: creates a resource — not idempotent; calling twice may create two records
PUT: full replacement — idempotent; missing fields are nulled out
PATCH: partial update — idempotent if implemented correctly; only sends changed fields
DELETE: removes the resource — idempotent; first call returns 200, repeated calls return 404 but end state is the same

beats.text: Todo app: GET /todos returns the list (safe, cacheable). POST /todos with a body creates a todo (not idempotent — do it twice and you get two todos). PUT /todos/42 with a full body replaces the todo. PATCH /todos/42 with just status:done updates only that field. DELETE /todos/42 removes it. In Spring Boot: @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @PatchMapping, @DeleteMapping each wires one method. candidates miss: many candidates say POST is for all writes. It is not — POST is specifically for create. Updates belong to PUT or PATCH.

items: Using POST for updates — POST creates; use PUT or PATCH for updates
Confusing PUT with PATCH — PUT replaces the whole resource and nulls missing fields; PATCH updates only what you send

speakable_v2.cap: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH partially updates, DELETE removes. Safe = no state change. Idempotent = same result no matter how many times you call it.

question: What is idempotency and which HTTP methods are idempotent?
title: Idempotency in HTTP Methods
direct_answer: Idempotency means making the same request multiple times produces the same result. GET, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE are idempotent. POST is not — calling POST twice may create two resources.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of REST semantics beyond just knowing which method does what
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying PATCH is not idempotent — it is idempotent if implemented correctly
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why idempotency matters for retry logic in distributed systems

sections.title: Why Idempotency Matters
sections.content: Idempotency is critical for reliability. In distributed systems, network failures may cause requests to be retried. If a DELETE request is retried, the resource is already gone — that's fine, same end state. If a POST is retried, you might create a duplicate order or payment — that's a serious problem.

sections.title: Idempotency by Method
content: Idempotent: GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE, PATCH (when implemented correctly)
Not idempotent: POST (each call creates a new resource)
Safe (no side effects): GET, HEAD
POST idempotency workaround: Idempotency-Key header (used in payment APIs)
PUT idempotency: sending PUT /users/1 {name: 'John'} 100 times always results in {name: 'John'}
DELETE idempotency: first call returns 200, subsequent calls return 404, but end state is same — resource is gone

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: Idempotent means you can make the same request many times and the outcome is the same as making it once. GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent — deleting a user twice still leaves no user. POST is not idempotent — submitting an order form twice could charge the customer twice. This matters for retry logic: if a network request fails and you don't know if the server received it, it's safe to retry GET or DELETE but dangerous to retry POST without an idempotency key. Payment APIs like Stripe use Idempotency-Key headers to make POST safe to retry.

followup_questions: How does Stripe handle POST idempotency?
What happens when you retry a DELETE and the resource is already gone?

seo.metaTitle: HTTP Idempotency Explained | Java Backend Interview
seo.metaDescription: Learn which HTTP methods are idempotent and why it matters for REST API design. Fresher prep.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API for a todo app with GET, POST, PUT, DELETE endpoints
speakable_v2.hook: Idempotent means you can hit the same endpoint ten times and the outcome is identical to hitting it once — that's what makes retries safe.

beats.text: Idempotency means calling the same operation multiple times produces the same end state as calling it once. It's a promise about repeatability. GET, PUT, DELETE, and (when correctly implemented) PATCH are idempotent. POST is not.

Networks fail. A client that doesn't know if its request reached the server needs to retry. If the operation is idempotent, retrying is safe. If it isn't — like POST creating an order — retrying may charge the customer twice. Idempotency is the foundation of safe retry logic.

items: GET: idempotent and safe — reading a todo list 100 times gives the same list
PUT: idempotent — replacing todo 42 with the same body 100 times leaves the same todo
DELETE: idempotent — first call removes the todo and returns 200; later calls return 404, but the end state (todo gone) is identical
POST: not idempotent — calling POST /todos 100 times creates 100 todos
PATCH: idempotent if your implementation merges cleanly; can become non-idempotent if it appends rather than replaces

beats.text: Payment scenario: user clicks Pay twice due to a slow network. If your payment endpoint is POST /payments, you may charge twice. The fix is an Idempotency-Key header — the client sends a unique key; the server stores the result for that key and returns the same response on duplicates. Stripe uses exactly this pattern. non-obvious: idempotency is about the end state, not the HTTP response code. DELETE returning 404 the second time is still idempotent — the resource is gone either way.

items: Saying PATCH is always non-idempotent — it depends on your implementation; a merge-patch is idempotent
Thinking idempotency means same response code — it means same end state; DELETE returning 404 on a repeat is still idempotent

speakable_v2.cap: Idempotent = same end state no matter how many times you call it. GET, PUT, DELETE are idempotent. POST is not. Use Idempotency-Key headers to make POST safe to retry.

question: What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?
title: PUT vs PATCH
direct_answer: PUT replaces the entire resource — missing fields become null. PATCH updates only the specified fields, leaving others unchanged. Use PATCH for partial updates to avoid accidentally nulling out fields.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the practical difference and when to use each
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using PUT for partial updates, accidentally clearing fields
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention JSON Patch (RFC 6902) for complex PATCH operations

sections.title: PUT vs PATCH Semantics
sections.content: PUT is a full replacement. If you have a user with {name: 'John', email: 'john@gmail.com', age: 30} and you PUT {name: 'Johnny'}, the result is {name: 'Johnny', email: null, age: null}. PATCH sends only what changed: PATCH {name: 'Johnny'} gives {name: 'Johnny', email: 'john@gmail.com', age: 30}.

sections.title: Key Differences
content: PUT: full replacement — client sends complete representation
PATCH: partial update — client sends only changed fields
PUT requires client to know entire current state
PATCH is more efficient — smaller request payloads
In Spring Boot: @PutMapping vs @PatchMapping
JSON Patch (RFC 6902): structured format for PATCH operations [{op: 'replace', path: '/name', value: 'Johnny'}]

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: The difference is scope. PUT replaces the entire resource — if you don't include a field, it gets cleared. PATCH only updates what you send. In practice, most APIs use PATCH for updates because it's safer and more efficient. You only send what changed. In Spring Boot, you use @PatchMapping annotation. One thing to watch out for: PATCH requests in Spring Boot can be tricky because request body binding will set fields to null if not provided — you often need to merge the existing entity with the patch manually.

followup_questions: How do you implement PATCH in Spring Boot without nulling other fields?
When would you still prefer PUT over PATCH?

seo.metaTitle: PUT vs PATCH HTTP Methods | Java Backend Interview
seo.metaDescription: Understand the difference between PUT and PATCH for REST API updates. Java fresher prep.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API for a todo app with GET, POST, PUT, DELETE endpoints
speakable_v2.hook: PUT says send everything, PATCH says send only what changed — pick wrong and you silently wipe data.

groups.label: PUT
groups.text: PUT replaces the entire resource. The client sends the full representation. Fields not included in the body are nulled out on the server.

groups.label: PATCH
groups.text: PATCH sends only the fields that changed. The server merges those changes into the existing resource, leaving other fields untouched.

items: PUT: when the client always has the full resource and wants to replace it atomically — like overwriting a config object
PATCH: when the client updates one field — like marking a todo done — and shouldn't need to re-send the whole object

beats.text: Todo with title, description, and done flag. PATCH /todos/42 with body {done: true} marks it complete and leaves title and description as-is. PUT /todos/42 with body {done: true} would null out title and description — probably not what you wanted. In Spring Boot, @PatchMapping maps the PATCH verb. The tricky part is the merge logic: you load the existing entity, apply only the non-null fields from the request, then save.

speakable_v2.cap: PUT = send everything or risk nulling fields. PATCH = send only what changed. Most update endpoints should be PATCH.

question: What are safe HTTP methods and why does the distinction matter?
title: Safe HTTP Methods
direct_answer: Safe methods are those that don't modify server state: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS. They can be called repeatedly without side effects. Browsers and proxies may freely cache or prefetch safe requests without concern.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding the contract between HTTP methods and intermediaries
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing safe with idempotent — all safe methods are idempotent but not vice versa
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain how browsers use the safe/unsafe distinction (e.g., not preloading DELETE links)

sections.title: What Makes a Method Safe?
sections.content: A method is safe if it doesn't change resource state. GET /users/1 just reads — no change. DELETE /users/1 removes — not safe. This distinction matters because browsers and crawlers know they can follow GET links freely. If a GET link triggered a delete, that would be catastrophic (and is why CSRF attacks target state-changing methods).

sections.title: Safe vs Idempotent
content: Safe methods: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS — read-only, no state change
All safe methods are also idempotent
Idempotent but not safe: PUT, DELETE — change state but same result if repeated
Not safe, not idempotent: POST — changes state and not safe to repeat
Browser prefetch: only prefetches safe URLs
CSRF tokens: only needed for unsafe methods that change state

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: Safe methods — GET, HEAD, OPTIONS — don't change server state. Browsers exploit this: they can preload pages linked with GET without worrying about side effects. All safe methods are also idempotent, but the reverse isn't true. PUT and DELETE are idempotent but not safe — they change state, just predictably. POST is neither safe nor idempotent. This distinction matters for things like CSRF protection — you only need CSRF tokens for unsafe methods like POST, PUT, and DELETE.

followup_questions: Why are CSRF attacks typically against POST not GET?
Can GET requests have side effects in practice?
What is the OPTIONS method used for?

seo.metaTitle: Safe vs Idempotent HTTP Methods | Java Backend Interview
seo.metaDescription: Learn safe HTTP methods and why the distinction matters for REST APIs. Java fresher interview prep.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API for a todo app with GET, POST, PUT, DELETE endpoints
speakable_v2.hook: Safe methods don't change server state — browsers and proxies exploit that promise in ways that affect your app.

beats.text: A safe HTTP method is one that doesn't modify server state. GET, HEAD, and OPTIONS are safe. Calling them has no side effects — nothing is created, updated, or deleted. All safe methods are also idempotent, but not all idempotent methods are safe.

Browsers, crawlers, and proxies treat safe methods as read-only. A browser can preload a linked page with GET without concern. A proxy can cache GET responses. If GET could trigger a delete, the web would break every time a search engine crawled your site.

items: Safe and idempotent: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS — read-only; no state change; cacheable
Idempotent but not safe: PUT, DELETE — change state but safely repeatable
Not safe, not idempotent: POST — changes state and calling twice may create duplicates
PATCH: idempotent if correctly implemented, but not safe — it modifies state

beats.text: In our todo app, GET /todos is safe — a browser can fetch it on every page load and cache it freely. POST /todos is not safe — a browser will warn before replaying it on refresh because replaying could create a duplicate todo. CSRF attacks target unsafe methods (POST, PUT, DELETE) because a forged request that triggers a GET causes no damage, but a forged POST could create or change data. Spring Security's CSRF protection only guards unsafe methods for this reason. production trap: some devs put data-changing logic behind GET endpoints for convenience — that breaks caching, makes bookmarks dangerous, and is a CSRF risk.

items: Confusing safe with idempotent — safe is a subset of idempotent; all safe are idempotent, not vice versa
Putting data-changing logic in GET endpoints — proxies may cache them, and browsers may prefetch them silently

speakable_v2.cap: Safe = no state change. GET, HEAD, OPTIONS are safe. All safe methods are idempotent — but idempotent doesn't mean safe. Browsers and caches rely on the safe guarantee.

question: How do you map HTTP methods to Spring Boot controller annotations?
title: HTTP Methods in Spring Boot
direct_answer: Spring Boot provides @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @PatchMapping, and @DeleteMapping annotations that map HTTP methods to controller methods. These are shortcuts for @RequestMapping(method = RequestMethod.GET) etc.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical Spring Boot knowledge alongside HTTP theory
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @PostMapping for updates or not knowing that @GetMapping can't have a request body
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show proper ResponseEntity usage and mention @PathVariable vs @RequestParam

sections.title: Spring Boot Method Annotations
sections.content: Spring Boot makes it easy to implement HTTP methods with dedicated annotations. Each annotation maps to the corresponding HTTP verb and handles request deserialization and response serialization automatically when combined with @RestController.

sections.title: Annotations and Usage
content: @GetMapping("/users/{id}") — read, use @PathVariable Long id
@PostMapping("/users") — create, use @RequestBody UserRequest body, return 201 Created
@PutMapping("/users/{id}") — full update, @RequestBody UserRequest body
@PatchMapping("/users/{id}") — partial update, merge with existing entity
@DeleteMapping("/users/{id}") — delete, return 204 No Content
Return ResponseEntity<> for full control over status code and headers
@RequestParam for query params: /users?page=0&size=10

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: In Spring Boot, each HTTP method has a corresponding annotation. @GetMapping for reads, @PostMapping for creates, @PutMapping for full updates, @PatchMapping for partial updates, and @DeleteMapping for deletes. I typically use ResponseEntity as the return type to explicitly control the status code — returning 201 Created after POST, 204 No Content after DELETE. For path parameters like /users/123, I use @PathVariable. For query strings like /users?role=admin, I use @RequestParam. These annotations are just shortcuts for @RequestMapping with a method parameter.

followup_questions: What is the difference between @PathVariable and @RequestParam?
When should you return ResponseEntity vs just the object?

seo.metaTitle: HTTP Methods in Spring Boot | Java Backend Interview
seo.metaDescription: Learn @GetMapping @PostMapping @PutMapping @PatchMapping @DeleteMapping in Spring Boot. Fresher prep.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API for a todo app with GET, POST, PUT, DELETE endpoints
speakable_v2.hook: Spring Boot has a dedicated annotation for each HTTP method — one annotation, one verb, no ambiguity.

beats.text: Spring Boot maps HTTP methods to controller methods using dedicated annotations: @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @PatchMapping, and @DeleteMapping. These are composed shortcuts for @RequestMapping with a specific method parameter, reducing boilerplate to a single annotation per endpoint.

Before these shortcuts, you had to write @RequestMapping(method = RequestMethod.GET) on every method. Spring 4.3 introduced the composed annotations to make controllers more readable and reduce typing.

items: @GetMapping("/todos") — handles GET; use @RequestParam for query filters like ?done=false
@PostMapping("/todos") — handles POST; use @RequestBody for JSON input; return ResponseEntity with 201 CREATED
@PutMapping("/todos/{id}") and @PatchMapping("/todos/{id}") — handle updates; use @PathVariable for the id
@DeleteMapping("/todos/{id}") — handles DELETE; typically returns ResponseEntity.noContent() for 204
ResponseEntity — use it when you need to set the exact status code, not just return the body

beats.text: Full todo controller: @GetMapping returns List of TodoResponse (Spring auto-serializes to JSON via Jackson). @PostMapping with @Valid @RequestBody CreateTodoRequest returns ResponseEntity.status(201).body(saved). @PatchMapping with @PathVariable Long id and @RequestBody Map of String to Object applies partial update. @DeleteMapping returns ResponseEntity.noContent().build(). sharp edge: @GetMapping technically can receive a body but most HTTP clients and servers ignore it — never rely on a request body in GET; use @RequestParam for query parameters instead.

items: Using @PostMapping for updates — POST creates; updates belong to @PutMapping or @PatchMapping
Forgetting ResponseEntity and returning the object directly — you lose control over status codes; Spring defaults to 200 even for creates

speakable_v2.cap: @GetMapping reads, @PostMapping creates (return 201), @PutMapping/@PatchMapping updates, @DeleteMapping removes (return 204). Always use ResponseEntity to control status codes.
